L57@P0: 1. Introduction and Overview
L58@P0: Natural language processing (NLP) has developed rapidly over the last decades. It has a wide range
L59@P0: of applications, including speech recognition, optical character recognition, text categorization and
L60@P0: many more. The theoretical analysis has also advanced significantly, though many fundamental
L61@P0: questions remain unanswered. One clear challenge, both practical and theoretical, concerns deriving
L62@P0: stochastic models for natural languages.
L63@P0: Consider a simple language model, where the distribution of each word in the text is assumed
L64@P0: to be independent. Even for such a simplistic model, fundamental questions relating sample size to
L65@P0: the learning accuracy are already challenging. This is mainly due to the fact that the sample size is
L66@P0: almost always insufficient, regardless of how large it is.
L67@P0: To demonstrate this phenomena, consider the following example. We would like to estimate
L68@P0: the distribution of first names in the university. For that, we are given the names list of a graduate
L69@P0: seminar: Alice, Bob, Charlie, Dan, Eve, Frank, two Georges, and two Henries. How can we use this
L70@P0: sample to estimate the distribution of students’ first names? An empirical frequency estimator would
L71@P0:

L73@P1: assign Alice the probability of 0.1, since there is one Alice in the list of 10 names, while George,
L74@P1: appearing twice, would get estimation of 0.2. Unfortunately, unseen names, such as Michael, will
L75@P1: get an estimation of 0. Clearly, in this simple example the empirical frequencies are unlikely to
L76@P1: estimate well the desired distribution.
L77@P1: In general, the empirical frequencies estimate well the probabilities of popular names, but are
L78@P1: rather inaccurate for rare names. Is there a sample size, which assures us that all the names (or
L79@P1: most of them) will appear enough times to allow accurate probabilities estimation? The distribution
L80@P1: of first names can be conjectured to follow the Zipf’s law. In such distributions, there will be a
L81@P1: significant fraction of rare items, as well as a considerable number of non-appearing items, in any
L82@P1: sample of reasonable size. The same holds for the language unigram models, which try to estimate
L83@P1: the distribution of single words. As it has been observed empirically on many occasions (Chen,
L84@P1: 1996; Curran and Osborne, 2002), there are always many rare words and a considerable number
L85@P1: of unseen words, regardless of the sample size. Given this observation, a fundamental issue is to
L86@P1: estimate the distribution the best way possible.
L87@P1: 1.1 Good-Turing Estimators
L88@P1: An important quantity, given a sample, is the probability mass of unseen words (also called “the
L89@P1: missing mass”). Several methods exist for smoothing the probability and assigning probability
L90@P1: mass to unseen items. The almost standard method for estimating the missing probability mass
L91@P1: is the Good-Turing estimator. It estimates the missing mass as the total number of unique items,
L92@P1: divided by the sample size. In the names example above, the Good-Turing missing mass estimator
L93@P1: is equal 0.6, meaning that the list of the class names does not reflect the true distribution, to put
L94@P1: it mildly. The Good-Turing estimator can be extended for higher orders, that is, estimating the
L95@P1: probability of all names appearing exactly k times. Such estimators can also be used for estimating
L96@P1: the probability of individual words.

L98@P1: 1953, 2000). It has been extensively used in language modeling applications since then (Katz, 1987;

L149@P2: 1.2 Logarithmic Loss
L150@P2: The Good-Turing estimators are used to approximate the probability mass of all the words with a
L151@P2: certain frequency. For many applications, estimating this probability mass is not the main optimization criteria. Instead, a certain distance measure between the true and the estimated distributions
L152@P2: needs to be minimized.
L153@P2: The most popular distance measure used in NLP applications is the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. For a true distribution P = {px}, and an estimated distribution Q = {qx}, both over some
L154@P2: set X, this measure is defined as ∑x px ln px

L160@P2: Many NLP applications use the value of log-loss to evaluate the quality of the estimated distribution. However, the log-loss cannot be directly calculated, since it depends on the underlying
L161@P2: distribution, which is unknown. Therefore, estimating log-loss using the sample is important, although the sample cannot be independently used for both estimating the distribution and testing it.
L162@P2: The hold-out estimation splits the sample into two parts: training and testing. The training part
L163@P2: is used for learning the distribution, whereas the testing sample is used for evaluating the average
L164@P2: per-word log-loss. The main disadvantage of this method is the fact that it uses only part of the
L165@P2: available information for learning, whereas in practice one would like to use all the sample.
L166@P2: A widely used general estimation method is called leave-one-out. Basically, it performs averaging all the possible estimations, where a single item is chosen for testing, and the rest are used
L167@P2: for training. This procedure has an advantage of using the entire sample, and in addition it is rather
L168@P2: simple and usually can be easily implemented. The existing theoretical analysis of the leave-oneout method (Holden, 1996; Kearns and Ron, 1999) shows general high probability concentration
L169@P2: bounds for the generalization error. However, these techniques are not applicable in our setting.

 | Glossary Biotic similarity A measure of the degree to which two or more samples or assemblages are similar in species composition. Familiar biotic similarity indices include Sørensen’s, Jaccard’s, Horn’s, and Morisita’s indices. Hill numbers A family of diversity measures developed by Mark Hill. # Measuring and Estimating Species Richness, Species Diversity, and Biotic Similarity from Sampling Data

## Abstract and Figures

This article reviews modern statistical approaches to estimating species diversity and biotic similarity from empirical samples of species abundance or incidence. Key methods include rarefaction, extrapolation, and non-parametric estimation of the asymptote of species richness. Hill numbers are presented as unifying indices of species diversity that take into account the relative abundance of different species. Species richness estimators, Hill numbers, and measures of biotic similarity can be extended to account for phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional diversity of biological assemblages. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
